He finished his work on the code after he had finished his paper — and in the process came up with the modified Huffman coding idea, which is quite a bit more efficient than what he discussed in the paper. It started with a routine feature in ScopeDB: implementing approx_count_distinct for approximate distinct counting. HyperLogLog (HLL) is the standard textbook choice. Early on, Rust’s HLL ecosystem was uneven, so I started with Cloudflare’s open-source cardinality-estimator . That crate leaned heavily on unsafe code and manual bit-packing tricks, though, so to keep things auditable and under our control, I forked and maintained an internal copy inside ScopeDB. While evaluating alternatives, I came across Apache DataSketches, which offered a battle-tested HllSketch alongside CpcSketch, an even more space-efficient design. At the time, Apache DataSketches only shipped Java and C++ implementations, whereas ScopeDB is written in Rust. As it turned out, the Apache DataSketches community was interested in an official Rust port. Starting late last year, I teamed up with a few other Rust developers well-versed in sketching algorithms to build and ship the initial releases of datasketches-rust, beginning with HllSketch. Soon after, I switched ScopeDB’s distinct counting over to our datasketches-rust implementation. Anyone who has implemented streaming distinct counting knows how HLL works: elements are hashed into K K K buckets, and each bucket keeps only the maximum leading-zero count seen so far (typically 4 to 6 bits), while every other hit in that bucket goes unrecorded. Once HLL enters dense mode, every bucket maintains a fixed-width register. In his 2017 paper Back to the Future: an Even More Nearly Optimal Cardinality Estimation Algorithm , Yahoo! Research scientist Kevin J. Lang proposed going back to basics: instead of keeping only per-bucket maxima, retain the full K × 64 K \times 64 K × 64 bit matrix of the classic FM85 coupon collector’s process. Whenever row r r r sees a hash with c c c leading zeros, set bit ( r , c ) (r, c) ( r , c ) to 1 1 1 . Keeping the full two-dimensional hit matrix lets CPC pair a streaming HIP estimator with a mergeable ICON estimator for higher statistical efficiency than HLL. On serialization, it adapts its layout to fill density: low cardinalities use a sparse PairTable of (row, column) pairs, while medium and high cardinalities combine a sliding 8-bit window, length-limited Huffman coding, and column permutations to pack the sketch near the information-theoretic entropy limit. According to the DataSketches documentation, serialized CPC shrinks storage by 30% to 40% compared with HLL at equal accuracy. In late January, I ported CpcSketch to datasketches-rust ( PR-75 ) and switched ScopeDB over to it. It has run smoothly in production for more than six months. While porting CpcSketch from the upstream C++ and Java implementations, however, I noticed several hardcoded magic lookup tables in the source code: These four sets of static tables live in compression_data.rs and estimator.rs . So I opened ISSUE-720 on datasketches-java to ask where the generator sources lived. Lee Rhodes replied: Kevin did most of his math simulations and modeling in OCaml. And his code was on his computer, which no longer exists. And his personal code died with him … even if they have a copy of his old computer it might be trying to find a needle in a haystack. Kevin passed away in April 2019, and any code left on his personal machine is effectively lost to history. I was saddened to hear that. Kevin’s research in sketching algorithms underpins many of the core sketches in Apache DataSketches: Still, with the runtime decoders and detailed header comments sitting right there in the source files, it seemed possible to reverse-engineer the offline generators from the artifacts alone. I asked Lee whether the CPC paper explained how the tables were derived, and he answered: You should definitely read the paper. But it won’t tell you any details on the Huffman codings. As I recall, in his paper he used a more standard compression scheme. He finished his work on the code after he had finished his paper — and in the process came up with the modified Huffman coding idea, which is quite a bit more efficient than what he discussed in the paper. That placed the derivation well beyond what I could work out on my own in an afternoon. Since CpcSketch worked fine in datasketches-rust as long as the lookup arrays were copied faithfully, I left the mystery aside for the time being. Then Gemini 4 Carbon came out just as I was preparing the next release of datasketches-rust. Since the checked-in tables and 20-digit header comments already acted as a strict numerical oracle, any candidate generator could be tested immediately in code: either it reproduced every codeword, permutation entry, and floating-point diagnostic within IEEE-754 precision, or it was wrong. That made the problem well suited to an agentic workflow built around executable checks and adversarial review. Over several iterations, I steered three models against that oracle and against one another: None of the models got everything right on the first try, and several plausible-looking explanations collapsed as soon as we tested perturbations in code. What survived that filter became PR-355 , which checks the reconstructed generators and derivations into datasketches-rust as unit tests, following the same approach we took for kxp_byte_lookup . The rest of this post focuses on the mathematics and numerical forensics behind those four sets of tables: how each structure works, which wrong turns looked convincing until an ablation broke them, and where the surviving artifacts cannot tell two models apart. Formal derivations sit in the appendix at the end; if you spot an error, feel free to leave a comment or open a PR on datasketches-rust. We begin with the 23 Huffman coding tables in compression_data.rs . Why hardcode 23 static Huffman tables at all? Building trees dynamically per sketch would force the serializer to write tree headers into the compressed stream, wiping out the tens of bytes saved on small sketches. Meanwhile, the probability that column j j j of the coupon matrix is set depends mainly on the fill ratio C / K C / K C / K (collected coupons C C C over row count K K K ). Precomputing optimal tables offline across representative C / K C / K C / K checkpoints lets determine_pseudo_phase select the right table solely from lg_k and num_coupons without storing a table ID. To be clear, the million-trial Monte Carlo simulator and raw trial outputs were kept locally as an independent verification record rather than checked into the PR. The reconstructed generators, closed-form constants, and hardened tests have been merged upstream in PR-355 . Writing those unit tests underscored an important engineering lesson: never write tautological tests . An earlier draft verified the asymptotic constant against a second hardcoded copy inside the test file, and checked confidence bounds only by testing whether they bracketed the point estimate. Simple mutation testing exposed both gaps immediately: changing the production constant to a coarse 0.794024 or zeroing out all 132 confidence-table entries still passed every test. We hardened the merged tests in two ways: the constant test calls production code directly to compare the runtime constant against the closed form, and the confidence-table test asserts strict monotonicity of interval width with kappa while stating its verification limits explicitly in comments. Today, all 23 Huffman tables and 16 permutation tables have bit-exact constructive tests, whereas the Monte Carlo confidence tables clearly document that unit tests do not verify empirical cell values or true coverage. When reverse-engineering legacy numerical code, the biggest trap is thinking, “all tests pass, so we recovered what the author wrote.” Proving a model reproduces the artifacts is not proving the author coded that model.
